Every nonzero number raised to the power.why: A school rule stated in many forms ('x^0 = 1', 'to the power of 0 is 1', 'to the zero power is 1'); Wikipedia gives it as the definition of a zero exponent.

sources.quote: A number raised to the 0 power is generally defined to be 1

sources.query: to the power of zero is one

A spreadsheet cell that raises a nonzero.why: A spreadsheet setting the rule has to be carried into; no text states what such a cell shows.

sources.query: spreadsheet AND to the power of 0
cell AND raised to the power 0

For a nonzero number x, x raised to the.why: A two-step computation on a fresh variable: no text states the result; the rule gives x^0 and the multiplication follows.

The square root of 9 is 3..why: A basic square root, stated often.

Zero is a positive number..why: False in standard English usage: zero is neither positive nor negative.

sources.quote: Conversely, a number that is greater than zero is called positive; zero is usually (but not always) thought of as neither positive nor negative.

sources.query: zero is neither positive nor negative

A nonzero number w raised to the power 0.why: A made-up two-step computation on a fresh variable w: nobody writes what is left after subtracting w^0 from 10. Its premise (a nonzero number to the power 0 is 1) is the kind of thing people say all the time, while the final result of this particular computation is not the kind of thing anyone states on its own; the rule gives w^0 and the subtraction follows.

notes: TBox contraction paired with mathematics-replace-0006: removes 'every nonzero number raised to the power 0 equals 1'. The three derived queries name a spreadsheet value v, a fresh variable x (times 5) and a fresh variable w (subtracted from 10), so no stored fact about a named number offers a route back; the rule is the only route (inheritance, 2 hops with the membership in the prompt). The propositional negation asks 'a nonzero number raised to the power 0 does not equal 1' (no, then unknown).
